messages.subject: Re: likert item scale
parts:
a simple way to check is run the analsys without changing your original scoring.
don't reverse the values 
keep 4 for none of the time in both factors
if you are right about the constructs being inverse to each other then a high score 4 on distress should be inversely correlated with well-being items. 
but as it stands you have reversed well-being so a high score (all of the time) positively correlates with a high score for distress (none of the time); perfectly logical

On Saturday, 5 July 2025 at 11:42:46 UTC+12 Sara wrote:

This is my survey

Respondents were asked the following questions:

1.                How often have you been a nervous person?

            How often have you felt calm and peaceful in the past month?

              How often have you felt downhearted or blue?

             How often have you been a happy person?

           How often have you felt depressed?

Each item was rated on a four-point Likert scale indicating frequency:
1 = All of the time, 2 = Most of the time, 3 = Some of the time, 4 = None of the time.

I have a methodological concern regarding the treatment of the response scale. Initially, I recoded the items so that

- for distress-related items (nervous, down, depressed) , I left  “1” as “ All of the time ”, 2 = most of the time, 3= some of the time and “4” as “ None of the time.” 

- for well-being items (happy, calm), I reversed the scale so that “1"indicated “ None of the time  ” , 2 = some time, 3= most of the time and 4 =  All of the time  .”

Then , For these well-being items , I inverted the response scale by recoding 1 as 4 and 2 as 3, and vice versa, 

 The goal was to ensure that lower values consistently reflected psychological distress and higher values reflected well-being.  

  However, after running a confirmatory factor analysis with two correlated latent factors—Well-Being and Distress—the resulting correlation between the two factors was positive (r = 0.81). This raises concerns, as I would theoretically expect a negative correlation between psychological well-being and psychological distress.  Was my approach correct, or did I do something wrong?

messages.author: 5d76fb0f37513f01
messages.subject: Re: likert item scale
parts:
Thanks for answering.

data2010 <- new_data[, c("YSAQ_282C_2010", "YSAQ_282D_2010", "YSAQ_282E_2010", "YSAQ_282F_2010", "YSAQ_282G_2010")]


model_two_2010 <- '
  Well_being =~ YSAQ_282D_2010 + YSAQ_282F_2010
  Distress =~ YSAQ_282C_2010 + YSAQ_282E_2010 + YSAQ_282G_2010
 '


fit_two_2010 <- cfa(model_two_2010,
                    data = data2010,
                    ordered = names(data2010),
                    estimator="WLSMV",
                    std.lv=T)




summary(fit_two_2010,fit.measures=TRUE,standardized=T)

Now, the correlation between the two latent factors—Well-Being and Psychological Distress—now appears negative (-0.79) , as theoretically expected. However, the robust RMSEA remains relatively high in the two-factor model. Notably, I also tested a unidimensional model, but the robust RMSEA for that solution was equally high. I don't undersatnd why this happens. The index values are shown in the attached image

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: likert item scale
parts:
I will go out on a limb a little bit. The drivers of your robust CFI and RMSEA scores are going to be (1) the constraints of your mCFA being inconsistent with the data; (2) the distribution of your data deviating from what one would expect given an underlying multinormal distribution; and (3) sample size. Keep in mind also that expectations for the values of fit indices rely on a certain "typical" model--they are not customized to your model. "Dynamic" fit index thresholds, achieved through simulation, might give you a better basis for evaluating your results.
     Your model is pretty simple and should yield only 4 degrees of freedom. The CFA model only requires that each of the 5 items load only on the assigned factor and that all shared variance across items be mediated by those factors. So less-good fit index values suggest that something else is going on. I can imagine that, with such closely connected psychological constructs, there may be cross-loadings, correlated residual variance or items mis-assigned to factors.
     I notice that your "robust" values for RMSEA and CFI are less good than the original values. Typically, excess kurtosis in data causes robust values to be adjusted to indicate better fit. But if data show the opposite--too little kurtosis versus what would be expected from underlying normality--then the opposite happens. Look at histograms of your data--are they flat or maybe U-shaped, rather than especially peaked? Alternatively, do you have miscoded missing data or careless responses? (I doubt this last one, given the high factor correlation.) That could explain both the lack of fit and the behavior of the robust fit indices.
     As noted above, CFI and RMSEA behave "as expected" only for certain ranges of sample size, given model complexity. Is your sample size especially large or small? Your choice of estimator also relies on very large sample size, so if sample size were small, that would again explain a great deal of what you are seeing.

messages.subject: Re: likert item scale
parts:
You may have multiple populations combined in this dataset. It might take distinguishing the populations, maybe via mixture modeling, in order to obtain the expected fit.
     Or you might try sacrificing information by recoding that item as binary, combining all response categories other than "never."
     Certainly, your sample size is well outside the range of most modelers' typical experience, spo "dynamic" fit thresholds may be valuable for you.
McNeish, D., & Wolf, M. G. (2023). Dynamic fit index cutoffs for confirmatory factor analysis models. Psychological Methods, 28(1), 61.

This is my survey

Respondents were asked the following questions:

1.                How often have you been a nervous person?

            How often have you felt calm and peaceful in the past month?

              How often have you felt downhearted or blue?

             How often have you been a happy person?

           How often have you felt depressed?

Each item was rated on a four-point Likert scale indicating frequency:
1 = All of the time, 2 = Most of the time, 3 = Some of the time, 4 = None of the time.

I have a methodological concern regarding the treatment of the response scale. Initially, I recoded the items so that

- for distress-related items (nervous, down, depressed) , I left  “1” as “ All of the time ”, 2 = most of the time, 3= some of the time and “4” as “ None of the time.” 

- for well-being items (happy, calm), I reversed the scale so that “1"indicated “ None of the time  ” , 2 = some time, 3= most of the time and 4 =  All of the time  .”

Then , For these well-being items , I inverted the response scale by recoding 1 as 4 and 2 as 3, and vice versa, 

 The goal was to ensure that lower values consistently reflected psychological distress and higher values reflected well-being.  

  However, after running a confirmatory factor analysis with two correlated latent factors—Well-Being and Distress—the resulting correlation between the two factors was positive (r = 0.81). This raises concerns, as I would theoretically expect a negative correlation between psychological well-being and psychological distress.  Was my approach correct, or did I do something wrong?
